newsitem.title: USA: Carter says Israeli plan may bring violence.
newsitem.headline: Carter says Israeli plan may bring violence.

text.p: Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter said on Wednesday that Israeli plans for a new Jewish neighbourhood on the southern edge of East Jerusalem could lead to renewed violence between Palestinians and Jews.

Speaking to reporters before the arrival of Palestinian President Yasser Arafat for a meeting at the Carter family residence in rural south Georgia, the former president also said he was ready to help facilitate the troubled Middle East peace process if called upon.

"Building mass numbers of settlements precipitates the possibility of violence," said Carter, whose administration set the region on the road to peace in 1979 by helping forge the Camp David accord between Israel and Egypt.
"It couldn't be a more serious and more focused issue in Jerusalem," he added.

Arafat was three hours late in arriving from New York because the pilot of his Saudi Arabian jetliner got confused about the destination and brought the plane down at an airport near Atlanta, 180 miles (290 km) to the north of Plains.

Before leaving New York, the Palestinian leader had told U.N. Security Council members that Israel was harming the Middle East peace process by its plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, one of the towns now under Palestinian self-rule.
The building site, on land captured by Israel in the 1967 Mideast War, is called Har Homa by the Israelis and Jebel Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians.

Speaking to reporters after conferring privately with members of the 15-nation council, Arafat said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "pushing the peace process in very critical and crucial circumstances."
"They are saying it is Har Homa settlement. The target is to replace Har Homa instead of Bethlehem and to separate Jerusalem from Bethlehem," he said.
The Palestinian leader's stay in Georgia lasted less than an hour before he left for a meeting with former President George Bush in Houston.

During a brief press conference at the Carter home, Arafat praised the former president's work through the Carter Centre, an Atlanta-based think tank devoted to conflict resolution, democratic reform and Third World humanitarian projects.
